what: An MCP server exposes tools, resources and prompts to AI apps through the Model Context Protocol, one open standard. Build it once and any MCP host - Claude, an IDE, your own agent - can use it.
like: Like a USB-C port for AI: one standard plug, so any app can connect to any device without a custom cable for each pair.
why: Write one integration instead of one per AI app and model
Tools, data and prompt templates arrive with names, descriptions and JSON schemas the model can read
Clear security edges: OAuth scopes, per-server isolation and a human who can say no

nodes.t: Your API or DB|where work happens

steps.d: The host app creates one MCP client per server and keeps the whole conversation. Each server sees only what it needs, never other servers or the full chat.
The client calls tools/list and gets each tool's name, description and input schema. These land in the model's context, so descriptions act like search snippets the model ranks.
stdio: the host runs the server as a subprocess and swaps newline-separated JSON-RPC messages. Streamable HTTP: one endpoint taking POST and GET, with optional SSE streaming.
A remote server answers 401 and points to its metadata. The client runs OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, naming this server as the resource, and asks only for needed scopes.
On tools/call the server checks the token's audience and scope, validates inputs, applies rate limits, then does the real work against your API or database.
Results go back as text or structured content. Errors use isError so the model can fix its arguments and retry. Every call is logged for audit.

numbers.l: standard transports: stdio and Streamable HTTP
each MCP client talks to exactly one server
tokens saved in Anthropic's code execution example: 150k to 2k
missing or bad token vs missing scope (insufficient_scope)
suggested length of a tool name, in characters

choices.d: stdio for a local server on the user's machine: simple, no network port. Streamable HTTP for a shared remote server with many users, sessions and OAuth.
A few task-shaped tools beat one tool per API endpoint. Clear names and descriptions decide whether the model picks the right one.
Hundreds of definitions eat context. Load them on demand with a search_tools tool, or expose them as code files the agent reads and calls.
Start with a small read-only scope and step up when a write is first needed. Check tenant id from the token on every call, never from tool arguments.
Rate limit per user and per tool, cap result sizes, and set timeouts, so a looping agent cannot flood your backend.

instead.why: One app, a few tools: define them in code, no protocol needed
Plain REST clients, not AI hosts: a normal gateway is enough
Let the agent write code that calls tools, saving tokens
Risky actions get a person's yes before the tool runs

breaks.d: Dozens of servers load hundreds of tool definitions, crowding context and confusing selection.
breaks.see: Large prompt tokens before any work; tool-selection accuracy falling in evals
breaks.fix: Load tools on demand (tool search), fewer task-shaped tools, sharper descriptions

breaks.d: A tool description or result carries hidden instructions the model follows, such as sending data elsewhere.
breaks.see: Unexpected tool calls or data flowing to new destinations
breaks.fix: Allowlist servers, scan and pin descriptions, treat outputs as data, confirm sensitive calls

breaks.d: The server forwards the client's token to a downstream API instead of using its own.
breaks.see: Downstream logs cannot tell which client acted; audits get muddy
breaks.fix: Accept only tokens issued for this server (audience check); get separate downstream tokens

breaks.d: One token grants every tool, so a leak exposes everything.
breaks.see: Tokens carrying wildcard scopes like files:* or admin:*
breaks.fix: Minimal starting scopes, step-up on demand, tenant checks server-side

breaks.d: A model retries a failing call again and again.
breaks.see: One session sending hundreds of identical tools/call requests
breaks.fix: Per-user rate limits, timeouts, clear isError messages so the model changes course

say: I'll wrap our search API as a remote MCP server on Streamable HTTP, with a handful of task-shaped tools instead of one per endpoint.
Auth is OAuth 2.1: the server checks each token was issued for it, and tenant and scope come from the token, never from tool arguments.
Tool descriptions are effectively a retrieval corpus for the model, so I'll evaluate tool-selection accuracy and load tools on demand when the list grows.
Every call is rate limited and logged, and anything that writes or sends data asks a human first.

followups.a: stdio for local tools: the host launches the server as a subprocess, credentials come from the environment. Streamable HTTP for shared remote servers: one endpoint, sessions via Mcp-Session-Id, OAuth, and Origin checks against DNS rebinding.

followups.q: How would you pick the right tool among 500?
followups.a: Treat it as retrieval: index tool names and descriptions with BM25 plus embeddings, give the model a search_tools tool, and load only the top few definitions. Measure tool-selection accuracy on a labelled set of tasks.

followups.q: Why does code execution with MCP save tokens?
followups.a: Tools become code files the agent reads only when needed, and big intermediate results stay in the sandbox. The model sees just the final summary, so a 150,000-token workflow dropped to about 2,000 in Anthropic's example.

followups.q: How do you keep tenants apart?
followups.a: Bind every request to the user and tenant in the validated token, scope data queries by that tenant id, key sessions as user plus session id, and never trust ids passed in tool arguments.

today: The 2026-07-28 MCP spec recommends Client ID Metadata Documents for registering clients and marks Dynamic Client Registration as deprecated, kept only for older authorization servers.

check.q: Who decides when an MCP tool is called?
check.a: The model, with a human able to deny
d: The MCP server, on a timer
check.why: Tools are model-controlled; the spec says a human should be able to refuse an invocation.

check.q: Your server receives a token issued for another API. What should it do?
d: Accept it if it has not expired
Swap it for a session cookie
check.why: Servers must only accept tokens issued for themselves; passthrough is forbidden.

check.q: Which transport fits a local server on the user's laptop?
check.why: The host launches it as a subprocess; nothing listens on a network port.

check.q: A tool fails because a date is in the wrong format. How should it report that?
check.a: A result with isError: true and a clear message
check.why: Tool execution errors reach the model so it can fix the arguments and retry.
